Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to remind the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) of the past but since she is doing it herself and seems delighted to do so, I must stand up and speak out as well. I think that the Hon. Member for Outremont was involved in the issue of the status of women because of the Axworthy case, when the minister responsible for the status of women in the former government told women who wanted equality that they had better postpone their intervention on the Constitution and the Charter of Rights so as not to undermine the political standing of his party. I had the privilege, Mr. Speaker, to attend that conference and ... I see some other women across the way who were also present... and fortunately, in spite of the fact that the previous Liberal minister wanted to establish priorities that were not in line with those of Canadian women, we still have been able to do our job.
As a second reminder of the past, since she is pleased about it again, the federal Government has imposed its will on the provinces, it argued with them, did not respect their independence and their responsibilities and their rights, though they represent the Canadian citizens as much as the federal Government; because of this lack of respect for another level of government, progress has been slowed down on many issues, including women's issues. The Hon. Member, for instance, refers to the amended legislation on the rights of native people saying that despite the efforts of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie), the children of some native women who will at last be equal under the law will not recover their rights. But she forgets to indicate that this responsibility falls upon the Native Nations themselves and not the Government. Those nations will decide what the status of people living on Indian reserves will be.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to point out those inconsistencies and oversights, some of which are certainly unintentional. Moreover, I wish to refer to another inconsistency. The Hon. Member said that the Minister had got his fingers burnt when he met with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and vice versa. She should make up her mind. Well, if it is so, it is because something has changed. I also want to remind her, since she has reminded us that amendments to the Divorce Act were brought about in part by the previous administration, although most of the new provisions are very different from the old ones, I want to remind her that it is the Clark Government which, in 1979, introduced the new concept of spouse's allowances and that this government quickly moved, after its election, to extend this benefit to widows and widowers between 60 and 64 years of age. We would certainly want to give much more to all the elderly poor, but it is a spouse's allowance. It would amount to extend family allowances to older people because they are poor. Our programs must be consistent.
Second, the previous administration had not earmarked any funds for the elderly, so that we had to establish a fund in an attempt to offer at least this allowance.
Therefore, I wish that in her passionate effort to defend the achievements of the previous administration, the Hon. Member really remembers where all these things came from. Mr. Speaker, I also want to ask her whether when she was appointed to the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, she found the job more pleasant than Mrs. Doris Anderson did when she was there.

I welcome this opportunity to reply to my colleague because I feel that anyone who indulges in personalities at this time cannot have much to say for women. We are here to pass legislation on women's issues, not to make personal remarks on each and every one of us. However, I am very happy to tell you that, as regards Section 15 of the Charter of Rights, I can still claim that we worked very hard at that time to have it adopted, and the Council played a very important role. The Council is also responsible for having Section 28 passed and for organizing all provincial and women's groups so that pressure could be brought to bear on all three parties.

speechtext: Questions or comments? Debate. The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald).

Mr. Speaker, the Government is blamed today for its policy related to Canadian women. We are asking for concrete measures aimed at improving the status of women. Indeed, the Conservative party, when they were in opposition and especially during the last election campaign, promised such measures. Yet they have not kept their promises since then. On the contrary! Their policies since the election have been prejudicial to women. Let us first consider tax reform. This Conservative Government has maintained the federal tax increase proposed last year by the Liberals. This Conservative Government has found billions of dollars for oil companies, including multinationals. The Conservative Government did not fill the loopholes in the tax system, which benefit private corporations. The Government has even admitted that the most recent loophole with regard to research expenses is costing Canada more than $1 billion each year. Yet the Government could not find money to meet the needs of Canadian men and women. The old age security benefits, for example, could have been increased with that amount of money.
To pay for those hand-outs to private corporations, the Government had to save elsewhere. In fact, the Government has chosen to cut in the budgets of departments and Crown corporations like the CBC. Given that situation, women are
Supply
those who get laid-off. Women who just recently got a job are laid-off. For instance, the budget cuts in research on the environment, ill-advised to start with, have particularly cost women their jobs.
This Government has a policy or rather an ideology favouring the private sector at the expense of the public sector, no matter what the consequences are for Canadian men and women. It follows that some jobs in the public sector are cut in favour of private sector growth. The growth of the public sector favoured women in Canada. This sector has been growing and giving good jobs to women since the Second World War. The men-women salary differences are smaller in the public sector. Social benefits are better, pensions, union protection, etc., are better. Now, women's jobs are threatened the most by the present policy of the Conservative Government. Unfortunately, the Government is blinded by its ideological concerns. Women are more practical and less interested in ideology. They are interested in the quality and the value of the jobs involved rather than in which sector they fall.
Women who came before the NDP job action group talked to us very specifically about this point. They talked about the need for good jobs, the fact that these jobs had developed especially for women in the public sector. Unions had fought for women and got better working conditions and salaries, and because of the ideological preoccupations of the Government these are the jobs that are cut back. The Government does not realize that there are particular implications for women in a policy which might seem to be gender-free. A policy of protecting the private sector and attacking the public sector has very serious implications for women.
The National Action Committee on the Status of Women in Canada is very aware of these difficulties. Indeed, one of its major recommendations resulting from its conference this past weekend concerned precisely this point. I would like to read that recommendation to the House. It reads:
Whereas the value of tax concessions allowed by the federal Government is between 30 and 50 billion dollars per year according to the Auditor General; and whereas these tax breaks benefit large companies and high income tax payers the most; and whereas this situation is largely responsible for the deficit; and whereas the deficit is now being used as an excuse to cut public spending; and whereas women are the first to be hurt by such cuts; be it resolved that NAC lead a campaign strongly recommending that the deficit be reduced through reform of the tax system and not through public spending cuts.
This is precisely what the NDP has been urging, along with many other organizations. I note the Economic Council of Canada, not known to be a great supporter of the NDP, recommended that this approach be taken rather than cuts in public spending.
I want to go on to some more specific matters in the resolution before us today concerning job creation and job training programs. We in the NDP believe that these must be specifically targeted to women. We do not believe that the laws of nature are favourable to women in that sense. We have seen that neglect means that the status quo continues. Women

May 13, 1985
Supply
are disadvantaged in the labour market right now and, without precise means of intervention, that disadvantage will continue. For that reason we recommend that in job-training programs paid for out of public funds, sponsored by Government, 50 per cent of the places be accorded to women. Young men and young women come into the labour market in roughly equal numbers, and for training purposes women should be getting half those places. For job-creation projects involving public money, women make up roughly 42 per cent of the labour force, a growing percentage at that, and jobs should be reserved for women in that proportion. That is only fair. Unfortunately, to date we have seen the Government take the view-and I am sorry to say the previous Government had the same view-that the real jobs are men's jobs. The construction job which ends with some kind of physical object, be it building a bridge or what have you, is a more real job than a service job providing daycare and nursing or educational services. The kind of jobs women do in communities have not been valued as being worth much and women have not got as much support in job-creation programs. To prefer these capital-increasing projects over human resource-oriented projects seems to be a gender-free approach, but in fact it is not. It means that men's jobs are preferred to women's jobs.
We recommend that the Government develop effective action programs. By "effective" we mean programs with numbers, goals and deadlines. The Abella reforms, which were practical and fairly modest-one certainly cannot call them revolutionary-have only been partially respected in the Government's response. It has not gone far enough. I point out that the National Action Committee recommended a much more vigorous approach to the Government's response to the Abella report, and indeed the NAC condemned as inadequate the planned legislation in response to that report. The NAC instead urged the federal Government to introduce programs and practices through affirmative action with mandatory requirements, enforcement, numerical objectives and deadlines to bring about equality under federal jurisdiction.
Why do we need to have numerical quotas and deadlines and very precise measures? Because it has not worked otherwise. We have had kind words about affirmative action, plans and programs for action. As arts and culture critic, let me refer you to one in my own area. The CBC is a Crown corporation. Back in 1970, the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada recommended that Crown corporations have a special responsibility and that they design their own program for improving the participation of women. That was 15 years ago. Well, they were not forced into doing it, there were not numerical quotas, and eventually, after a great deal of pressure, they came up with vague plans. But of course there has been very little change in the proportion of women in management or producers' roles, and there has been even less change in the portrayal of women on the screen. The record has not been good because there has not been accountability, and I think we have to say, enough of plans for action, enough lip service, we want some real action. We want evaluations, and if they are not satisfactory, then fire the people responsible and we will replace them with people who will take equality for women as a serious objective.
Regarding evaluation, I can recommend the McDonald "no fudge factor". This is a statistic which I think all of our government Departments and Crown corporations, and indeed private corporations with contracts with the Government, should be required to publish. Specifically, this would mean that each Department would publish the proportion of women on the payroll. This of course could be pro-rated for part-time workers and the proportion of the payroll they get. If we see that in a certain area women were 60 per cent of the payroll but they got only 40 per cent of the pay, we would know that most of that payroll was going to the smaller number of men who had the supervisory jobs or jobs which were evaluated at a higher level. Then we could have year after year that same proportion and we could see very objectively if the proportion of women in those jobs was improving. It would not just be up to the government Department to talk about how good its attitude is toward women and how much it was proposing to do but in fact not doing.
I would like now to turn to the question of equal pay for work of equal value, a very important and integral part of any kind of job equity plan for women. We have it at the federal level on paper. We have the Canadian Human Rights Commission enforcing it, and I would like to say that it is doing the best enforcement in Canada on this principle. Unfortunately, I cannot say that it is all that great because there have been numerous delays, it has not been vigorous in the pursuit of some cases, its guidelines are a little backward and out of date, and I think it could be making further progress.
If equal pay for work of equal value had been vigorously implemented at the federal level, it would show up in the statistics. We could look at the industries regulated at the federal level, and the regulations have been in place for about seven years now, and we would see over the years declining differences in wage and salaries within industries at the federal level. Unfortunately, statistics do not show such a trend. Implementation has still been haphazard and based on a case by case complaint system, and it still takes years for cases to be resolved. I would point to the Bell Canada case and that made by the communications workers of Canada. The Canadian Human Rights Commission has not been vigorous. It has accepted excuse after excuse on the part of the employers. We have seen no progress despite quite a bit of pressure from women's organizations in support of the women who are being discriminated against in these particular places of employment.
The guidelines of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, which have recently come out, show some improvement in some respects, but they are inadequate in others. It is a step forward and a step backward. I would like to point out a few of the deficiencies. It is very important that small and large groups be compared for the purpose of dealing with actual cases. The fact that a woman with a complaint is in a badly outnumbered job category is no reason why she should not
May 13, 1985

have her day in court or before the Canadian Human Rights Commission. It is no reason to deny her coverage by the Canadian Human Rights Act. Complainants need more information and cases should be more speedily processed. There should be a flexible definition of establishment. There have been improvements here, but it is still not good enough.
Of course that only opens up the question of extending this coverage of equal pay for work of equal value to the private sector and to all companies which are under provincial jurisdiction but which do business with the federal Government. This is an enormous opportunity because the federal Government is a major purchaser of goods and services of companies of all sizes across the country. This is an opportunity for the Canadian Human Rights Act to have a much greater impact. It can tell companies that if they want to do business with the Government they will have to pay people according to this principle. That must apply to all contractors rather than only a small number of them.
I am pleased to see that this issue was raised in the Ontario election. It was interesting to see the Ontario Conservative Party, under the pressure of an election campaign, suddenly decide that equal pay for work of equal value was a good idea, as least for government employees. It would not go so far as to say that it was fair for all employees. Its time has come, Mr. Speaker. It is a matter of elementary justice that women's jobs be fairly evaluated. Simply adhering to the old market principle is not good enough. Women have been discriminated against for far too long in the job market. Equal pay for work of equal value is the way to address the problem of ghettoiza-tion and the downgrading of women's jobs. Objective criteria must be the basis for comparisons, to have fair rates of pay.
I would like to address one further matter which is raised in our motion today, that is the provision of transition houses and funding for them. It is absolutely essential that there be regular funding for transition houses. Violence against women exists. We would like to stop it, it will be some time before this does happen. It is an ongoing problem for which there must be a regular means of funding. The voluntary sector puts much time and effort into keeping these transition houses alive. In serving women in crisis, they are always in dire need themselves. There is always some problem of funding. They spend much of their time rushing around trying to keep the organization together and the service going for women who suffer enormously in our society. It is time we had regular, decent funding, making it possible for these groups to provide the services needed without having to fight for their existence every fiscal year.
I will close by simply pointing out that equality for women is a real challenge for us today in Canada. Providing equality for women in the workforce requires a certain amount of intelligence but, more than that, it requires a lot of political will. We know what needs to be done. Lack of implementation rather than lack of ideas is responsible for the fact that we are not making adequate progress right now. Token appointments and vague promises are not enough. They are totally inadequate.
Supply
There are enough women to share equally in the work of our major regulatory agencies. There is no reason why they should remain at the 24 per cent level when women make up 50 to 52 per cent of the population. That is the level they should be at. That should be the case now rather than in the future.
We have seen that vague promises have not worked in the past. We want concrete measures with implementation, deadlines, and evaluation. The barriers do remain. It is the responsibility of Government to act vigorously to reduce these barriers. They are not going to go away without us taking our responsibility seriously, bringing in better legislation, and providing adequate funding for the necessary services. Equality for women is a question of justice. Canadian women want to play their full role in society. Canadian women want equality in the family and in the economy. We are far from achieving it. Let us move toward it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak to the resolution before the House on the continuing economic inequality of Canadian women. The resolution points to a situation that is well known and fully acknowledged by all Members of the House and by all sectors of Canadian society. The economic inequality of women in this country is a reality that none of us are proud of. Lower average income, the ghettoization in occupations that are low paying or threatened by technological or economic change, inadequate pension coverage, and unequal opportunity in hiring, promotion, and training are barometers of economic inequality.
This is not to denigrate the important gains which women have made in recent years. These, such as the equality clause in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, are quite significant. However, many of these gains are still in the pioneering stages. The first doors have been opened and the first toe-holds gained, but the vast majority of women have not yet been touched. In fact, in difficult economic times there is a dangerous temptation to roll back the progress which has been achieved. I can assure my colleagues that the Government is committed to resisting that temptation and to pressing forward with the changes required to achieve equality.
Today's debate affords a very useful opportunity to acknowledge and applaud the efforts of those working to make equality for women a reality. Thousands of women across the country are devoting their time, energy, expertise, and in many cases their hard-earned dollars, to ensure that this necessary work gets done. They are working through organizations and as individual citizens. They are doing valuable research and analysis, often breaking new ground for the rest of Canadian society. They are developing an understanding of the causes of inequality and arriving at workable solutions to overcome these problems, thus leading the way for public and private decisionmakers. All of this lays the groundwork for our deliberations here in this Chamber.
The Government applauds and supports the work of these organizations. Many of them have been meeting here in Ottawa over the past weekend under the auspices of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. NAC is well known to the Members of the House. Many of us went to hear it this morning. That afforded us an opportunity to hear the views of this umbrella organization. Although NAC is not always in agreement with the policies of the Government, as we heard this morning, its views and opinions are always a welcome contribution to the democratic process. I might say that groups such as that can be most effective if they put forward their views in a civil and co-operative manner. Through NAC and many other large and small organizations
across Canada, men and women from every walk of life are working for economic equality. I believe that the vast majority of Canadians support their endeavours.
However, there are always some difficulties with progress and some temporary bumps in the process as we smooth out the transition period. I know that a few Canadians are opposed to equality. They are nervous about change and uncomfortable with society's inexorable progress toward equality. This is a natural human response to uncertainty, but it is no reason to balk at the task. Our Government is fully committed to full equality for women, as we believe most Canadians are, and we will not stray from that commitment.
The resolution before the House speaks to several aspects of economic equality for women. There are also many other elements that we have heard raised in the debate today that are important to this discussion. One of the most useful instruments for achieving economic and social equality will be the equality rights clause, Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This Charter is helpful as a yardstick for legislators to remind us of our obligations in all legislation that we deal with and to ensure fair and equal treatment of all Canadians, regardless of sex, race and other grounds.
As Members know, and as I certainly am becoming aware, it is not a simple task. Legislation, regulations, programs and policies which, on their face, do not appear to be discriminatory may in fact have different impacts on different segments of the population. In addition, the time honoured practices of discriminatory treatment may appear to many of us, by force of habit, to be logical and sensible, whereas, in fact, they are unconscionable.
We must be clear that many sacred cows will be gored in the horns of the equality clause, but they will clear the way for a more fair and equitable Canadian society.
To assist the process of revising existing legislation, much of which will have a direct impact on women's economic equality, the Government has launched a process of consultation with Canadians. I am pleased to be a member of that special committee which will open its hearings across the country in several weeks. Already we have been hearing from organizations here in Ottawa on a wide range of issues which are being put to us. I am sure that the House will consider all of the views which we put forward in our report to it, prior to final decisions on legislative amendments.
However, as we all know, the legislative process is not in and of itself sufficient to ensure the implementation of the equality clause. One of the other important steps is the development of judicial interpretations as to what the equality clause actually means.
Many organizations representing Canadian citizens will be using the courts to obtain clear legal precedents on this matter. Litigation is an expensive and time consuming process, and particularly difficult to undertake for those who are most disadvantaged in our society and precisely the people who will want to bring cases before the courts. The Government recog-
May 13, 1985

nizes the obstacles that these groups face in bringing their cases before the courts and also recognizes the importance of test cases. Consequently, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) has indicated on previous occasions, the Government is considering financial assistance to those groups seeking equality under the Charter, including women as well as racial minorities and the disabled.
Let me take this opportunity to commend those women who have taken the initiative in this area and established the Legal Education and Action Fund, or "LEAF". Many of us went to the kick-off party on April 17 to promote women's legal equality, including via the Charter. This organization will be needed in the coming years.
There are other areas in which inequality is still with us. For example, action is needed at all levels of Canadian society to encourage and enable women to play a stronger role in setting up and running their own business. As I mentioned in the House last week, women now own 29 per cent of small businesses in this country. They are creating them at three times the rate of men and are playing a strong and significant role in this growing and important area of Canada's economy. Removing constraints on the development of new enterprises is a high priority of the Government and women stand to gain a great deal in that process. However, as in so many areas, this cannot be done by the federal Government alone. Greater access to credit and more institutional support at the community level is essential for women's success.
Much has been said about the fact that women form the majority of part-time workers. Yet these workers are often not treated on an equal footing with full-time workers. Employment counselling is a crucial step in the process of women's economic autonomy, and the federal Government is working to improve the quality of its service to women in these areas.
The six thrusts of the labour market strategy were designed to help Canadians, including Canadian women, obtain full and fair participation in the emerging labour market. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) advise the House earlier today that last month 47,000 women found jobs. That is the largest month-to-month increase in many years.
Equality for women is an important element of our labour market strategy. Many other elements of the strategy have been addressed elsewhere during this debate. However, we would be remiss if we confined our discussion of economic equality to women in the paid labour force. Although the majority of Canadian women are in the paid labour force, the majority of unpaid labour in this country is also done by women in the household and through voluntary organizations. The absolutely crucial job of raising children and running the domestic household is done almost exclusively by women and is done for free when they are doing this work for their own families.
The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women estimates that in families where the wife is a full-time homemaker, and the children are ten years of age or older, husbands do only three hours of housework a week. When this home-
Supply
maker takes a paid job outside the home, the husband's time spent on housework increases only by six minutes per week. It is also estimated that homemakers work about 40 to 60 hours per week, depending mostly on the number and age of their children. This work is equivalent to about 35 per cent to 40 per cent of the GNP, or at least $136 billion.
This represents a tremendous subsidization of Canadian society and is an economic contribution that is rarely recognized. We frequently pay homage to the social, emotional and psychological importance of the work of raising children and maintaining the support and love of the family unit. But how often do we acknowledge the economic importance of this work?
Obviously, the family benefits from the work of the homemaker, as do employers. Many Canadians believe that household tasks and the raising of children are responsibilities that should be shared by men and women. In practice, however, this sharing is very unequal. It is women, in the vast majority of cases, who carry the burden of domestic responsibilities. Men in Canadian society simply have not shouldered their share of these responsibilities. This must change if Canadian women are to achieve economic equality. As long as women carry the responsibility for unpaid domestic work and often the double burden of paid plus unpaid work, men will have an unfair advantage in the workforce.
There are other areas of concern. Most women expect that if they are widowed or divorced they will receive adequate benefits from their husbands' pensions. It comes as a shock to them to discover that in many cases they have no benefits at all. I know that according to the Public Service Superannuation Act, the divorced woman does not get the benefit of her husband's pension. If they do receive survivor pension benefits, these are often only a quarter of the couple's income.
Various proposals have been put forward by women's groups regarding the specific details of how best to incorporate homemakers into the Canada Pension Plan. These and other suggestions will be carefully considered by the Government in its deliberations. We intend to continue this discussion with the benefit of the views of a wide range of interested parties.
Any debate on the economic inequality of women must take account of the variety of women' experience in this country. Not all women face exactly the same barriers in exactly the same situations. Women as a group have many common experiences, yet various sectors within the population of Canadian women also have various experiences specific to them. For example, aboriginal women must deal with a gamut of economic obstacles which all women face, but they must also deal with racism and they must address economic issues from the point of view of aboriginal people.
Efforts by aboriginal people to develop their own economic base is fraught with problems, as the House well knows. The inadequate land base, the history of inappropriate training programs, the lack of infrastructure, and a whole battery of institutional and structural distortions in the economy of

May 13, 1985
Supply
aboriginal communities are just some of the problems. Women in these communities must deal with this entire layer of problems as well as with issues related to sex discrimination both within their communities and in dealings with the rest of Canadian society.
I have been privileged as a Member of the House to be involved in considering legislation to remove the imfamous sex discrimination in the Indian Act with regard to women losing their Indian status. The outcome of our committee's work will be put before the House very shortly. It will address the major issue of discrimination against Indian women, but it will not be a panacea for the woes of all Indian women. Those aboriginal women, whether status or non-status, reinstated or not, who live off-reserve face another series of obstacles in achieving economic equality. Racism and sex discrimination in employment, promotion, pay scales and any number of other areas are all very real problems for these women.
The Abella Commission inquiring into equality in employment in Canada recently estimated that over-all the unemployment rate for native women was double that for Canadian women. Similarly, these women earn on average more than 25 per cent less than Canadian women do over-all which, as we all know, is itself only a fraction of what Canadian men earn on average.
All these shortcomings point to the need for a specific approach to the economic equality of aboriginal women as part of an over-all commitment by Canadian society to equality for all women.
Visible minority women also face particular problems in seeking fair and equal treatment in the work-place. They encounter barriers both on account of their race and on account of their sex. They tend to be concentrated in certain types of job ghettos, usually low-paying, often non-unionized. I am sure Hon. Members are aware of the recent study in Toronto which tested the attitude of employers toward visible minorities. The actors, posing as job seekers, found that their chances of being offered employment were greatly influenced by the colour of their skin. If one adds to this racism the dimension of sexism, I think the picture of visible minority women becomes clearer. Not only do problems occur at the door when hiring decisions are being made, but also when opportunities for training, promotion and other career advancement are available.
Yet another area is the question of racial harassment, compounded for women by sexual harassment. Innuendoes, personal comments, offensive jokes and often harassing behaviour can make a workplace intolerable and essentially force a woman out of her only opportunity for increasing her economic independence.
The few areas on which I have touched are only some of those which concern the Government in matters related to economic equality for women. My colleagues and others will address other elements of this important debate today. Obviously one day is woefully inadequate to discuss these matters with the attention they deserve. It is no secret that these issues are a matter of continuing concern for this Government and
will be an important part of decisions related to economic recovery and renewal in Canada.
In closing, I would like to reiterate the importance of dialogue on these issues. We need to hear and learn from the women of Canada. We need to know their experiences, their triumphs and their frustrations as we work to establish an economic future for ourselves and for our daughters. I would like to encourage Canadian women, both as individuals and through organizations, to express their views to their federal, provincial and municipal Governments, to their unions, to their employers, to educational and training institutions, and to others in the Canadian community who have a role to play in achieving economic equality for women.
This Government will stand by its commitments, not the least of which is the commitment to listen to the women of Canada and to support them in their efforts to attain economic equality. We look forward to other partners in the Canadian economy doing the same.

Mr. Speaker, I have three specific questions for the Hon. Member. In light of her comments with respect to the involvement of women in small business and her knowledge that women need venture capital and the support of financial institutions like the Federal Business Development Bank, would she support my contention that the two vacancies currently available in the Federal Business Development Bank should in fact be filled by women? Will she be making presentations to cabinet in this regard?
My second question is to ask the Hon. Member whether she supports her Government's initiative to remove the pregnancy provisions from the current unemployment insurance package under federal law and to have it moved into general revenues. If so, how can she reconcile that position with her stated objectives of allowing women an opportunity to compete equally in the workforce?
Third, I know the Hon. Member has a vast knowledge of the political situation in British Columbia. Does she agree with the Leader of the British Columbia Progressive Conservative Party who was recently quoted on the subject of prostitution as saying that there was a need for prostitutes because men had a desire to procreate. He said: "It is the instinct of a male, particularly a young one, to procreate. And not to have that available creates a danger to society". This is what Peter Pollen, Leader of the B.C. Progressive Conservatives said. Does she support the view of her colleague, the Leader of the B.C. Progressive Conservatives?

Mr. Speaker, I will start with the last question First. I would like to dissociate myself totally from the remarks made by that man; I am not sure I could say gentleman. I am sure most of my colleagues on all sides of the House would join me in dissociating themselves from his remarks.
With respect to maternity leave, the proposals which have been put forward as potential areas of discussion do not in any way mean that there will not be maternity leave provisions for women in the workforce. Those are vital. In fact, the discussions have gone further to include parental leave, which per-
May 13, 1985

haps under the Charter makes more sense. Whether or not that should be funded directly out of the unemployment insurance fund or from general revenues, I do not think it really makes that much difference as long as they are there. My own view on unemployment insurance is that there are a lot of changes to be made in that fund to make it truly more of an insurance fund. Whatever changes are made, I would not in any way support removing or downgrading the enabling of maternity benefits for working women.
Finally, with respect to women on boards, particularly the FBDB, I assure my hon. colleague that I am continually making representations to my Cabinet colleagues and to others who are in positions to make appointments of women on all those kinds of boards. I think the Hon. Member will see from the record so far that we are making great progress. I am not yet satisfied, and I will continue with those representations.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad I was able to pick up on the debate specifically as it relates to the issue of maternity benefits and the current Government's recommendations to remove maternity benefits from unemployment insurance and place them under the aegis of general revenues. This particular measure by the Government since it assumed office on September 4 is a clear indication that it does not understand, not only the need for women to be allowed to compete equally in the workforce, but the recognition that child care or child rearing is in fact a cost of employment. It is a cost of employment which should be borne specifically under the unemployment insurance revenues of the federal Government. The move by this Government to take that envelope of spending out of unemployment insurance and to place it in general revenues speaks volumes about the lack of commitment to allow women to compete in the workforce. It is all well and good for government Members to say that the funds should remain the same. We know from historical experience and from the universality debate that if we take maternity benefits out of the unemployment insurance fund and move it into general revenues, we will be setting up another system, which could be described as a welfare system within the federal Government.
Very shortly thereafter we would see government proponents of deficit reduction saying to the Government that we have this pool of money going out to pregnant women across this country because they are unable to work during those critical child-bearing months, let us not allow that money to go out to all women but let us pay only those women in a position of dire and desperate need. In other words, very shortly after this Government chooses to remove maternity benefits from unemployment insurance funding, we will likely see the introduction of a means test for maternity benefits.
I suggest that those government Members who have a true and a well expressed commitment to equality for women must recognize that in order to achieve that equality, women need more support through instruments like the unemployment insurance funding. They do not need that support reduced in
Supply
the manner being suggested by current government policy on unemployment insurance benefits.
We have seen the same thing with respect to the new initiative by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to cut back on unemployment insurance to those senior workers who are receiving severance pay packages or vacation packages. We know that older women who are removed from the workforce face a tough enough time without having the added burden of being ineligible for unemployment insurance benefits until they have exhausted severance pay and holiday benefits.
We see Members on the government side of the House stand today and defend government policy which discriminates against older women who happen to be single or divorced. 1 speak specifically to the government legislation which will extend spousal benefits to those people between the ages of 60 and 64, the majority of whom are women, as long as they are widows, but will not extend the same benefits to those who have never married or who, for whatever reason, have suffered a marriage breakdown.
That particular discriminatory government policy introduced by this Government since September 4 clearly illustrates to the Canadian people that this Government is not prepared to fight for all women, and indeed all men, between the ages of 60 and 64, in particular our older workers. It is introducing legislation which sets up two classes of citizens, one that happens to have been widowed, and another that happens to be single or divorced. When I made my remarks relating to the comments made by the Progressive Conservative president in the Province of British Columbia, it was not totally tongue in cheek. In attitudes, not only in this House, but in the community, there is much work to be done.
I look at the labour dispute which is going on between Air Canada and its employees, who are in fact bargaining for a better deal under part-time and full-time employment. It was clear from the answers in the House today, not only from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) but also the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), that this Government has neither an understanding of the Wallace report on part-time work, nor an understanding of the fundamental recommendations of the Abella Commission which point the finger at the kind of ghettoization that Air Canada is encouraging in its current collective bargaining deliberations with the employees.
If we have a Crown corporation going to its employees and saying it will no longer put the cap on part-time workers but wants the right to employ 100 per cent part-time workers in the full knowledge that those part-time workers at the moment do not receive benefits similar to their full-time counterparts and, second, those employees will be paid less on an hourly basis, then that is sheer exploitation on the part of a Crown corporation, aided and abetted by the Minister, who has the gall to stand in the House and tell the union to go back to the bargaining table.
1 am sorry that the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight), in his weak-kneed approach to exercising a bit of Cabinet muscle, has not prevailed upon his colleague, the Minister of Trans-

May 13, 1985
Supply
port, to let him know that the Abella report was worth a little bit more than the paper on which it was written. If this Government has a true commitment to employment equity, it has an opportunity to show it four square before all Canadians by informing Air Canada that it will not allow unfettered part-time employment to the detriment of those on hourly wages and the further ghettoization of women who currently make up the majority of part-time workers of Air Canada.
Although the Government says that the issue is improving the status of part-time workers and although the Wallace report called for those improvements, the intention of the company in the Air Canada dispute is not to improve the lot of part-time workers. It is to allow free rein on cheap labour within the Crown corporation of Air Canada. Frankly, I am shocked and surprised that the Minister of Transport would enter into the debate and admonish the union when he does not have the facts in front of him. It would not be the first time this Government has stated one thing in its objectives-and the April 17 party was a wonderful thing-but when it had the chance to put its money where its mouth is, it had no voice.
I speak specifically to the challenges that will be coming from all parts of Canada with respect to the equality provisions as engendered in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Mr. Speaker, as you are no doubt aware, a fund has been set up called the LEAF fund, the Legal Education and Action Fund, to which all Members have been invited to contribute. It will permit women across this country who want to have access to the court system to determine once and for all what their status is with respect to equality in the work-place and equality on division of assets. Those women will be assisted by this fund. It is a sad situation when the Government of Canada refuses to allow independent funding of that kind of organization so that women and minority groups across this country can have a chance to put the Charter to use and to use it as one tool in the long fight toward economic equality.
The battle was begun a long time ago. It began in this House. I am happy to say that I am part of the Party that brought people into the House of Commons like Judy Erola, who was instrumental in including Section 25 as well as Section 15 in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I am happy to come from the region of Canada that produced politicians of the stature of Judy LaMarsh and Ellen Fairclough. The battle began many years ago with people like Agnes MacPhail and certainly Nellie McClung, politicians who broke through 10, 20 and 50 years ago. The work is still far from finished.
I picked up my local newspaper on Saturday when I was home in the riding. I had a chance to read about a conference going on with respect to the whole issue of violence in the family and wife assault. I read a comment in the newspaper that was made by one of the representatives of our local police force, a comment which will serve to illustrate how much work still needs to be done in this area. It was the view of this particular police officer that violence in the family was a two-way street and that it was not in fact the fault of the husband because there were many mitigating circumstances. I would like to read into the record the mitigating circumstances
to which he referred: "He knew of one case where a man beat his wife when he came home to a filthy house . . . Send the guy to a program for batterers ... and maybe send her to a program on how to keep house." This is the statement of someone who has, as part of his area of responsibility, the responsibility for pursuing the assaulters of women who parade under the guise of family violence. When we hear representatives of our law enforcement agencies making statements like that, we realize that there is much work to be done.
I do not have to remind the House of the response of the House of Commons to the original report on family violence headed by the former Hon. Member for Kitchener, Dr. Peter Lang. When that report was tabled, the response was guffaws. It has not been very long since we got the issue of family violence out from behind the closed doors of individual households and onto the public discussion table.
In the areas of family violence, Charter equality provisions and employment equity, if we are really committed to allowing women the opportunity to share equally in all of the good things that society has to offer, then we must be prepared to provide the financial commitment. That financial commitment includes not only cost-sharing agreements with the provinces but it also includes a commitment from the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to look at the funding of more interval houses and to include an extension to second-stage housing across this country.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite easy for us in Parliament to say that we would like women to achieve equality, but so far, the reality has proved that we are engaged in a fierce battle. When one speaks of equality, it is quite obvious, according to the Abella Report, that the government should require companies operating under its jurisdiction to have affirmative action programs. But, this would not mean much unless the government does empower the Canadian Human Rights Commission to enforce affirmative action programs within those companies. One realizes how hard it is for the Conservative members to entrust the Commission with fundamental powers to start proceedings against any private, public or semi-public companies which do not provide affirmative action programs in their operations because those members themselves did not support such programs in committee. One just has to read the proceedings of those meetings to know what they really think.

The following was attributed to Conservative Members of the House of Commons: "Constitutional protections for disadvantaged groups reflected in affirmative action programs threaten the rights of individuals, Conservative MPs told the Canadian Human Rights Commission Tuesday. Tory MP Chris Speyer who raised the concern when Chief Commissioner Gordon Fairweather appeared before the Commons Justice Committee warned that a preoccupation with group rights might result in reverse discrimination". Then we heard from the Tory MP for
May 13, 1985

Calgary East (Mr. Kindy) who said he is opposed to all affirmative action programs because he believes all capable people have equal opportunities in the work-place.

Mr. Speaker, payroll statistics are most eloquent since they show that on an average women earn 62 per cent of what men earn in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, women do not want a two-tier status whereby many capable women work in many places but are denied the opportunity to achieve "equality" because this government as well as other provincial governments, with the exception of the province of Quebec, are not prepared to recognize that equality between men and women in the work-place can only be achieved if we have equal pay for work of equal value.

It is not surprising to me that the Conservative Party has difficulty promoting affirmative action programs. It is not surprising to me that the Conservative Government has asked the Commissioner of Human Rights to do the impossible, to enforce affirmative action programs within the federal service without giving the Commissioner the legal teeth with which to carry out that enforcement. Those things are not surprising to me because there is a fundamental feeling within the Conservative Party that affirmative action is bad and somehow results in reverse discrimination.
I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the women of Canada are sick and tired of receiving 62 cents or 64 cents for every dollar earned by a man in this country. I am not foolish enough to rise in the House and say that any government initiative will reverse that trend overnight. However, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that initiatives which have looked at the question of equal pay for work of equal value, initiatives which the Government must use its political muscle to encourage provincial Governments across the country to implement, will in themselves close the wage gap by seven cents to 10 cents according to major economists who have studied the issue. There will be those among us who will say that equal pay for work of equal value will not solve the entire problem so therefore we should not implement it. However, this is a building-block process. One of the fundamental building blocks in that process is the implementation of equal pay for work of equal value.
I was not impressed by the half-hearted promise made by the Premier of Ontario in the eleventh hour, prior to the dawning of a new reconciliation, that he would implement equal pay for work of equal value within the Ontario Public Service. The question extends far beyond the Public Services of this country. There are too many people who are working in ghettoized jobs in the community who are not being touched by current federal legislation and who in fact are being left out of the provincial packages and even the meagre provincial packages suggested by people like the Premier of Ontario.
There will be those among us who will say that somehow we women have missed the boat because we prefer to take time off to have children or are not interested in advancement. However, we need only look at the dismal record of the education
Supply
sector in which women have played a singular role and have worked hard from time immemorial, not only regarding the informal teaching of our children but regarding the formal teaching through our education system. We can see quite clearly that, notwithstanding the admonitions of those who say that women have not achieved in the sciences and engineering sectors because there are not enough of us and we have not been there long enough, in the education sector, even though women comprise the majority of our educators across the country, the positions of public administration officials, school principals, vice-principals and positions of authority are still, in the main, allocated to men. This is happening at a time when women's participation in the workforce is increasing and at a time when education has been at the vanguard of the women's movement in terms of employment.
There is no doubt that we have many questions to address. 1 have touched on a few of them and I believe some other Hon. Members have touched on a few of them. I would like to say to the Government that if there is a message that came from the election held on September 4, it is that the women of this country have come of age. We are not prepared to take second-class citizenship on government delegations, committees and other things. I would suggest to all government Members that if they are truly committed to seeking equality for women, they should encourage their Minister of Employment and Immigration to take a firm stand to ensure that benefits accruing to women for pregnancy leave are not turfed out of the unemployment insurance fund in order that those benefits will not become another welfare benefit which will be cut by this deficit-reducing Government. A lot of women in the country are looking to the Government to provide leadership. That is an area which leadership can be shown.
I would encourage all government Members, who have spoken so well today on their commitment to employment equity and to the kinds of safeguards and development which we need to allow women to compete equally, to buttonhole their Ministers in the corridors of power and tell them that we will not stand for any move to shake women out of the unemployment insurance fund. In doing that, this Government would merely reinforce the notion that Conservatives are not interested in employment equity or affirmative action, but only in the maintenance of the status quo.

speechtext: Questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps). Her message came through loud and clear and I think that we all appreciated it greatly.
I detected a note of nostalgia for Queens Park. Perhaps we will have the next Ontario election campaign fought here as well.
I did appreciate her recognition that this is a deficit-reducing Government. That is a very important factor. But I would

May 13, 1985
Supply
like to join forces with the Hon. Member on a project which I believe she could support, and which I certainly support, that is, our lack of a key form of recognition for the famous five women who persevered in the Persons Case of 1930. The commemorative plaque which previously graced the entrance to the Senate Chamber is no longer there. I believe it ought to be restored to commemorate those famous five: Emily Murphy, Irene Parlby, Louise McKinney, Nellie McClung, and my dear lamented ancestor, Henrietta Edwards. I would be pleased to join with the Hon. Member in that venture.

Mr. Speaker, of course, I would support any move to recognize the famous five who determined, once and for all, that we women are persons. However, from a policy point of view, I would hope that our initiatives would move much beyond that. Sometimes when I listen to comments made by people such as the President of the Progressive Conservative Association of British Columbia, I wonder whether that recognition has permeated the skulls of some members of the political Parties.
The Member made reference to my nostalgia for Queens Park. I believe that if he had listened closely to my comments, he would have realized that I was attempting to give credit where credit is due, that is, to two jurisdictions across the country which have implemented legislation with respect to equal pay for work of equal value. Those two jurisdictions are the Government of Quebec and the federal Government, under legislation which was introduced by the Liberal administration. Unfortunately, 90 per cent of the workers in Canada are covered by provincial laws. No matter into what particular area of endeavour we launch out in the House of Commons, we will touch only those 10 per cent who are covered under federal laws, which include public servants and employees of Crown corporations and other companies which fall under federal law. That means that 90 per cent of the people of this country are covered under provincial laws. Unfortunately, Progressive Conservative-which is actually a contradiction in terms-Governments across the country have seen fit to ignore the overwhelming evidence which points to the implementation of equal pay for work of equal value as one in a series of strategies which would help bridge the salary gap between men and women.
I had felt that because of the unique relationship between the Prime Minister and the Premier of Ontario-although I am sure that relationship was somewhat shattered after the realities of May 2-those two Conservatives could have come together and provided an opportunity for those 8.5 million people in Ontario, 7.5 million of whom are not covered under federal law, for employment equity through provincial initiatives which would be encouraged by federal counterparts. We in the Liberal Party work together on those kinds of initiatives. When we form a Government in Ontario, we will work very closely with the federal Government. Unfortunately, it has been the history of the Conservative Party that federal and provincial Conservatives do not work together but, in fact, work against each other. I can understand why the Member
would not see the association between federal and provincial Governments.
It is very clear. My Party, its policies, and its positions have not altered from provincial to federal jurisdictions. I hope that the Hon. Member will encourage his provincial colleagues to come on side on this important issue because provincial jurisdictions currently cover those millions of Canadians who are not currently protected by the federal legislation which was introduced by the Liberal administration.

Mr. Speaker, while we are having a go at historical revisionism, I would like to point out the marvellous record of co-operation which existed for many years between the Liberal Government in Ottawa and the Liberal Government in Quebec. I would also like to point out the marvellous ideological compatibility which existed between the Liberal Government in Ottawa and the Government of the late Premier, Ross Thatcher, of Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, believe me, if we are looking at giving lessons in terms of ideological suicide, we only have to look across to the government benches of the House to see a number of Members who, in fact, have spent most of their lives destroying each other.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak today. The motion which is before us is important and brings an important subject to the attention of Parliament.
Of course, today is the day on which the National Action Committee on the Status of Women meets with all three political Parties. Its representatives are lobbying our caucuses and attempting to find out how far we are willing to go in terms of supporting the priorities which they established at their conference. We had an amiable meeting with them this morning and I know that the concerns which they raised with us are reflected in the resolution with which we are dealing today. Obviously, the resolution is focused on one area and the concerns of the women's movement are broader than that. However, the matters which are the focus of this resolution are important and essential matters.
The resolution deals with the economic inequality of women. We have all heard the statistics before, but it bears repeating that women who work in this country earn 60-cent dollars. In other words, the average income of a woman, with equal qualification to that of a man, is 60 cents, while the man earns one dollar. That continues throughout the woman's working life and into her retirement years, as the woman's retirement income is also based on 60-cent dollars. That is a grave and glaring injustice which continues in our economy and in the relationship between men and women. In addition, it bears repeating that the most visible poverty in this country, not only the economic inequality which pervades the whole of our economy-whether a woman is working in an area of modest income, middle income or upper income-is among women. I
May 13, 1985

think particularly of single parents. Single parent families live in the most acute poverty in Canada today, and 99 per cent of the time they are headed by women. Older women as well suffer from poverty, and the pension systems are still not adequate to meet their needs. So we are talking about a very real problem which results in very real human suffering when we focus the attention of this House on economic inequality of women and men.
I would like to comment on the three areas raised for us by the resolution, the over-all economic policy and the manpower policy of the Government. I must say in passing, Mr. Speaker, that it is ironic that even when we debate the inequality among men and women, when we seek that more attention be paid to the needs of women and we talk about job training and job-creation, we still use the term "manpower policies". Even the language falls short of our ideals and of human needs. Clearly we need more adequate language in order to express the ideals which we seek to realize.
1 would like not only to comment upon the Government's manpower policy but upon the whole question of public services, as does the resolution, and in particular the transition houses and daycare. In dealing with the over-all economic policy of the Government, and the other matters we want to bring before the House today, we must begin with the fundamental economic approach of the Government, which is to try to balance the books by way of cutting public spending. Hon. Members opposite would have us and the public believe that they have no choice, that they have no option but to cut back public spending, and to cut public spending in areas which hurt and do damage to the equality of women across this country. This is ironic in the sense that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), when he was Leader of the Opposition, entered into the women's debate, and one of the things on which he scored a lot of points was to lambaste the former Prime Minister for saying he had no option when it came to patronage appointments, for example. But now that he is Prime Minister of this country and leads the largest Party in this House, he comes before us with an economic policy that says, "We have no choice. We have to cut public spending and cut services which are essential and needed and which contribute to the equality of women".
I want to suggest there is a real option, and that is, tax reform. In other words, we have to look at the other side of the ledger. We have to look at our revenues and seek ways of increasing our revenues in a fair and equitable manner which will allow us to provide the services which will result in a greater equality among the men and women of this country. I will briefly suggest, Mr. Speaker, that one of the areas which really cries for reform is the way in which we distribute the burden of taxation between corporations and individuals. Any one who reads statistics with regard to our taxation policy will know that over the last couple of decades the burden of taxation, as it has been distributed between corporations and individuals, has shifted considerably and the burden is increasingly upon the shoulders of the individual taxpayer. Corpora-
Supply
tions in this country pay less and less of their share of the costs of running Government. In fact, corporations, when they do pay taxes, tend to get an almost equal amount back in terms of benefits for themselves from the Government. So, therefore, there is a potential for raising revenue in a fair way-revenue which we could use for essential services-from the corporations, if we were to insist that they pay their fair share and ensure that the burden of paying for Government would not fall totally upon the shoulders of individuals.
Another trend which has become evident in the taxation system over the last couple of decades is the distribution of the cost of Government between different levels of incomes of individuals. The taxation system has become less and less progressive. There are more and more tax write-offs and loopholes which allow upper-income Canadians to reduce their taxable income. Of course, the ordinary Canadian who has a simple pay cheque and no investment income has to pay the full burden of taxation because there are effectively no comparable loopholes for people at the lower levels of income. We need real tax reform in this country, Mr. Speaker. We need to arrive at a situation in which the taxation system in indeed truly progressive and which will ensure that upper-income Canadians pay according to their capacity to pay. That means that the upper-income Canadians will in fact pay more than people with more modest incomes.
This proposal as well came up in the last election campaign. It was brought up by my Leader in the form of a proposal for a minimum income tax. At that time he pointed out that in the United States such a tax exists. In the United States there is a minimum tax on upper incomes, which means, simply, that after one has added up all of the write-offs and tax loopholes which lawyers and accountants can put together, if the income comes down to below a certain point, there is still a responsibility to pay taxes and to help carry the burden of public services. That appears to me to be eminently reasonable and only fair and just. I mention the fact that this kind of tax exists south of the border to demonstrate that such a tax is feasible. It is possible to design such a tax and it is possible for an economy to run with such a tax in place. Obviously, the rationale for most of the tax loopholes in our taxation system has to do with economic activity. Each of the individual tax loopholes is there as an incentive to create economic activity and, therefore, it is justified in that way.
I agree with using the taxation system in order to stimulate economic activity, but when the taxation system is used in such a way that an individual can earn over $100,000 a year and still come before the taxation Department and indicate that he has no taxable income, then at that point we are no longer using the taxation system to stimulate economic activity. We are in fact abusing the system and creating an unfair tax system in which poor people have to pay tax and people who earn a great deal can find a way to end up paying no tax. That creates unfairness, injustice, resentment and alienation. So that issue needs to be redressed. It is an alternative to cutting needed public services, particularly those that relate to the equality of women. Those are at least two general areas in

May 13, 1985
Supply
which the Government couid approach tax reform in order to raise revenues to provide the services which are needed.
There is another suggestion I would like to make with regard to tax reform. It has to do with the reporting of tax expenditures. Something of which we need to remind ourselves from time to time is the fact that Government spends money in at least two fundamental ways. The Government can write a cheque, such as a family allowance cheque, and send it to a family, or it can give a grant to some organization or group, in other words, spend money in a direct fashion. The other way that Government spends money is by giving various forms of tax breaks or write-offs to corporations or individuals. It simply does not collect the tax it would otherwise be entitled to collect and thereby forgoes revenue. The problem with this kind of spending is that it is hidden. No one knows from day to day exactly how much we are spending in that way. Therefore, we need to have full and open reporting of tax expenditures. We need to acknowledge that we spend money every time we give someone a tax write-off. The full reporting of tax expenditures would give us an opportunity to examine their effectiveness. If ordinary Canadians became aware of just how much money we are spending in this way, then they would insist that those tax expenditures be effective, in other words, that they work. If their objective were to create employment, then they should create employment or else they would be eliminated.
I suspect there are many tax expenditures we could eliminate because they do not give us the economic benefit they promised and they do not create new employment. It is fairly obvious to most ordinary Canadians that if the tax expenditures worded by and large, then there would be many more ordinary Canadians working today than there are. So we on this side of the House recommend that the Government approach the problem of providing services from the perspective of raising revenue rather than of cutting those much needed services which deal with people's basic human needs and equality between men and women. So tax reform is something this Government must face up to.
More specifically, regarding the public service cuts themselves, let me say that when the Conservative Party campaigned during the election, it ran around reassuring people that, yes, it is going to reduce the deficit but it is going to do it by cutting out waste and fat. In no way is it going to touch needed and worth-while public programs. I wish to remind the Government and Members opposite of that commitment, a commitment which has been broken. It is time for Members opposite to look at those promises and the nature of the cuts they are making. They need to wake up and realize that Canadians are not going to accept cuts in needed programs and that if this Government continues to act the way it has, it will lose the public's confidence. Members opposite should remind themselves that one of the reasons they promised the Canadian people they would cut only waste in order to reduce the deficit is that they knew that if they were to tell the Canadian people they would cut valuable public services, Canadians would not put their confidence in them. They
should also realize, now that they are in office, that if they cut needed public services, Canadians will withdraw that confidence. So this Government should wake up before its own actions lead to its demise because of a lack of public confidence.
Another reason why these cuts in public services are ill advised is that, while I know the Government is doing this because it believes in its own way that it will reduce the deficit and lead to economic recovery, every time a cut leads to reduced consumer demand and unemployment, it also leads to reduced revenues for the Government. This is particularly true where the cuts affect services which are labour-intensive. So this Government's own economic programs could backfire and we could end up with a larger deficit.
One area of critical interest to the women's movement, and of course to all Canadians who are concerned with families, has to do with cuts as they affect social services, particularly the universality aspect. We should remind ourselves once again of what the Government said before it was elected. The Conservatives said that universality was a sacred trust. Even before election day, they said they would not touch medicare. Of course, medicare is of great concern to women across this country. Medicare meets family needs and Canadians will just not put up with a Government which tries to savage medicare. But once the Conservatives got into office, they issued an economic statement in which they questioned pensions and family allowances. Well, it did not take very long, maybe a month, for the Government to wake up and realize that it had better not fool around with pensions either, because Canadians were not going to allow a Government which ran on the promise of universality as a sacred trust to mess around with pensions. Canadians fought for these pensions over a long period of time and we are very proud of them as a social policy. But the Government has yet to give us any real assurances that it will not savage family allowances. The Government should realize, as it continues to tinker with and take apart the principle of universality in social programs in its effort to reduce the deficit, that family allowances are something that Canadians feel very strongly about. It took a long fight to get them for Canadians and they are something that Canadians will not likely give up.
So as we consider the equality of women today, we should consider that this Government should be very cautious as it approaches the question of family allowances. The Government should be more concerned about whether the level of family allowances is adequate and whether it can find ways of increasing benefits rather than trying to find ways to reduce or eliminate family allowances on the basis of income.
I see that my time is running out, Mr. Speaker, but I want to say that rather than approaching the whole question of how to pay for our public services, particularly those which relate to families and the equality of women, by way of cutting needed public spending, you should approach it from the revenue side and take a serious look at tax reform in this country. That is the way to raise the revenue to provide the
May 13, 1985

services that people need and which will lead to a better community and greater equality among men and women.
Mir. Caldwell: Mr. Speaker, I have enjoyed the debate this afternoon and I find it very interesting. However, no one mentioned just how much this deficit is costing us. No one spoke about what it costs each Canadian each day to carry this deficit, or the fact that 33 per cent of our taxes now go toward servicing our debt. Just think of the marvellous things we could do and the programs we could put into effect if one third of our taxes did not have to be used for paying interest on the national debt. I think it hurts many people, especially the women of this country, if we increase the deficit and the tax load. Many women with families will have to carry a heavier debt load. I am just wondering whether or not the Hon. Member would agree with the fact that carrying this deficit and increasing the tax load on all Canadians is hurting women.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should know that the way to reduce the deficit is by building a stronger economy. In order to do that we need a number of things. For example, we need an industrial strategy in the country. The Government has washed its hands of the economy. It wants to leave the economy to run itself. We are not going to have the wealth in the country to pay for public services and reduce the deficit if we leave things in that way.
We heard a good example today in the House when the Minister was answering questions with regard to Mitel. The Government has shown no concern whatsoever that an important high-tech industry, which is presently owned by Canadians, is going to be owned by foreigners. It seems to welcome the fact of a foreign takeover.
In order to have public services we must have a Canadian economy and policies that lead to the development of a Canadian economy. We cannot have economic growth in the country if our interest rates simply track American interest rates. We need a "made in Canada" interest rate policy. We need policies to support such a measure. However, the Government seems to be satisfied with leaving the economy to the decisions of the directors and bosses of private sector corporations. If we want to reduce the deficit, I suggest we do it by strengthening the economy and having policies which help us develop our economy, rather than simply leaving it to the private sector.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member did not point out the fact that all indications are that the economy is improving. Our interest rates are at their lowest levels in six and a half years. Inflation is down. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) announced 210,000 jobs in the last year and 47,000 jobs for women in the last month. How much more do you want to get our economy going? Housing sales have doubled. We may not have a "made in Canada" interest rate, Mr. Speaker, but interest rates are certainly lower than they have been for some time and the
Supply
economy is picking up. That is helping the women of the country to obtain jobs.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member seems to be satisfied with 11 per cent unemployment. There is no way that we in this Party would tolerate such a high rate of unemployment. The Government should not tolerate it either. We need a commitment from the Government for a full employment policy in the country. If the Government made that commitment in a real way and put all Canadians back to work, we would produce the revenues which would balance the books to enable us to provide essential services to Canadians.
The Hon. Member quoted a few statistics from the recent past. He seems to think that things are great in Canada for all Canadians. There are many Canadians who continue to be unemployed who need work. We need a serious commitment from the Government to provide work for all Canadians.
